question.worked_solution:
Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(1,2)$ and a general point $P(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{(x-1)^{2}+4}+2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2} \\  & =(x-1)^{2}+{(\sqrt{(x-1)^{2}+4}+2-2)}^{2} \\  & =(x-1)^{2}+(\sqrt{(x-1)^{2}+4})^{2} \\  & =(x-1)^{2}+(x-1)^{2}+4 \\  & =2{x}^{2}-4x+6.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=4x-4 & =0 \\ 4x & =4 \\ x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=4>0.$ Therefore, $x=1$ is a minimum of $S.$

Since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=1$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S\,(1)}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S\,(1)} \\  & =\sqrt{2(1)^{2}-4(1)+6} \\  & =\sqrt{2-4+6} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$
